title: Mumonkan 7 - Clean Your Bowl
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of taking care of oneself, others, and the world around us. By practicing mindfulness through zazen and becoming more aware of our thoughts, emotions, and surroundings, we can develop compassion for all beings and embody the Bodhisattva practice. This awareness can be cultivated through both instruction and personal responsibility, leading to a deeper understanding of ourselves and others, and ultimately transforming our relationships with the world around us.

sentences.text: **Shuko Edie Norton:** Good evening.
Nice to see everyone here.
We're going to talk about a koan.
Is this the second time we've done a koan series?
No, we're also going to talk about a koan.
Okay, this is the second time.
We're going to do a regular series.
I brought copies of the case and verse and so forth.
I've only got 20 though, so you're going to have to share them.
Pass them around and share with each other if you could.
The koan we're going to talk about this evening is Chao Chu, Wash Your Bowl.
Koans are stories that present fundamental perspectives on life and no life: the nature of the self and the relationship of the self to the earth, and how these interweave.
The study of koans helps us make personal what might usually be known only abstractly.
In a minute we'll read the koan statements and talk about them.
But first I want to introduce the two named characters in this koan.
Chao Chou, or Joshua in Japanese, known for the koan Mu, had the longest career of any Zen master.
He was born in 778 and became a student of Nan Chuan when he was 18 years old and remained with his teacher for 40 years until his teacher died.
After two years of mourning he became an itinerant student, seeking and talking with all the famous teachers of that time, asking them questions and also enlightening them as he went.
Finally at age 80 he settled down at a small temple and began to teach himself. [unclear: "That was students"] and he died at 120 years old, so he had quite a long career, a very famous fellow.
So the title of the koan is about him.
Then the other person who is named in this koan presentation is Wu Men, or Mu Man in the Japanese form.
He was a Sun dynasty Rinzai master and he lived at approximately the same time that our Soto Zen founder Dogen lived.
He worked on the koan Mu for six years, it is said.
Sometimes he was found pacing the monastery corridors at night and even banging his head against the pillars to try to get what Mu meant.
So it's a tough one to crack through.
Now please follow along as I read these aloud.
*The case: A monk said, "I have just entered the monastery, please teach me." said, "Have you eaten your rice gruel?"
The monk said, "Yes, I have." said, "Wash your bowl."
The monk understood.*
*Wu Men's comment: First, Xiao Shu opened his mouth and showed his gallbladder, his heart and his liver.
I wonder if the monk really heard the truth.
I hope he did not mistake the bell for a jar.*
And Wu Man's verse:
*Because it's so very clear, it takes so long to realize.
If you just know that flame is fire, you'll find your rice has long been cooked.*
These mysterious [unclear: "little hearts"] intrigue us and pull us into the story.
So what does this mean?
Wash your bowl means do what's necessary, what's needed.
Take care of what we use.
Take care of our environment.
Take care of our life.
Pay attention.
Be aware.
Don't look for mysterious meanings.
Meaning is in everyday activities and experience.
But this is a koan.
Surely there must be something more mysterious about it than this.
Some commentators have found some different and deeper meanings, like Xiao Shu was testing the monk to see where he was in his practice.
Or Xiao Shu was revealing himself completely, his gallbladder, his liver, his heart, and he was saying he was totally available to the monk.
But I like the simpler, more obvious interpretation: do what is needed.
The question is, how do we know what's needed?
How do we become aware of that?
In my experience, there are two main ways that that happens.
First of all, we're told what to do.
As children, we're told and shown how to put on our clothes, how to tie our shoes, wash our hands, feed ourselves, brush our teeth, make our beds, take the garbage out.
How to get to school on time, how to do algebra, how to learn how to write essays, et cetera.
Our parents and later our teachers show us what to do and how to do things.
They remind us and supervise us in all sorts of activities and skills.
When we first come to the zendo, we're told and shown how to sit zazen, facing outward, the wall.
How to sit on the zafu or the chair or the bench.
How to do gassho and when.
How to bow and when.
As we practice, we ask what to do with our busy minds and are given suggestions for how to just observe and how to let go of our thoughts.
As we continue to practice, we hear dharma talks and we read and listen to dharma as much and as rapidly as we can absorb it.
So this verse by Wu Man speaks to that: because it's so very clear, it takes so long to realize.
The second way that we learn what is needed is by taking responsibility for something: a task, a role, another person, a group of people.
This way is usually more effective for becoming aware of what's needed because we have bought in.
We've said, yes, I'll do this.
And we have agreed to be responsible for something.
We usually want to do a good job because it reflects on us, so we do our best.
When we take responsibility for the role of Tinken, like Ken over here, we want to learn how and when to strike the bell and the han and the mokugyo.
We're a little nervous because we might make mistakes.
So we practice and we do make mistakes, and we learn that it's okay to make mistakes.
By taking responsibility, we learn all the details of being the Tinken.
And this is the same with all the volunteer roles that we take.
When we're not in a special role, all of us practice washing our bowl when we get up to leave the zendo.
The appropriate action for each of us then is to tidy up our seating place.
We brush off our zabuton with our hands to get the lint off of it.
We plump the cushion on its end so it's all plumped back up, and we place it carefully, respectfully in the center of the zabuton.
In this way, each of us takes care of our surroundings, ourselves, and each other.
So in sum, we become aware of what's needed by being instructed and by taking responsibility.
Our zazen practice also leads us to seeing what's needed.
With zazen, we become aware of our thoughts and emotions and bodies, all of which speak to us as we sit.
Our practice is to notice what arises to our consciousness, to acknowledge it, and to let it go so that we can attend to each moment, moment by moment.
Over time, our minds become trained to be aware of more and more of our conscious and unconscious feelings and conditioned beliefs.
As we practice over the years, our awareness broadens so that we become aware of what's going on around and within us in our daily lives.
We become aware of a friend's resentment, though he tells us there's nothing wrong.
We become aware that two people might be having a relationship because we see them sneak quick looks across the room at each other.
That's fun.
We become aware that the speaker at a public meeting is actually really angry, though she says she's very optimistic.
We become aware of more things going on as our practice matures, as our awareness matures.
Oh, it's not that we finally get to know everything and why everything is happening.
That's much too complicated.
But our scope of awareness widens, and our connection with others deepens.
This doesn't always produce a happy outcome.

There are lots of things we'd rather not be aware of these days: politics, climate change, wars, and the terrible mass killings that continue to happen in our country and other countries, like the one in Orlando this week.
The world can be a painful place.
When our awareness is mature, we can't escape or hide from what is happening.
We become like Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of compassion who hears the cries of the world.
We hear them.
This is where our Bodhisattva practice to save all beings comes in.
The Bodhisattva practice is central to Zen practice.
The Bodhisattva is the enlightened being who could leave this troubled world and suffering, but who remains in order to help everyone become enlightened.
That's our vow: to be aware of what's happening and what is needed, and to help.
So the koan, wash your bowl, means not only take care of ourselves, but be aware of what others need and try to help.
This is the philosophical reason why in zazen we keep our eyes open, to be aware of everyone and everything around us.
If our eyes are closed in zazen and someone sitting next to us slumps over, we wouldn't know that he might need help.
We keep our eyes open so that we can live our Bodhisattva vow to be awake, to be aware, to wash our bowl when needed.
We have dedicated ourselves this evening to the tragedy of Orlando.
In doing so, we have taken the first step toward washing our bowl, becoming aware of a need.
We have gotten past denial that there is a problem.
This is a big step, an important step.
This is where Buddhism can help us and others, by not denying reality, by acknowledging that a problem is real, is ours.
We can help each other toward doing what's needed.
So what's next in this situation of mass killings in our country and in the world?
I invite you to comment tonight on how you're feeling and what your ideas are about what we could do about this.
First, I'll just say briefly what I have been doing.
I'm an action-oriented sort of person, so I got involved in gun control initiatives from several years ago.
I think probably the Sandy Hook tragedy really got to me terribly.
I've written to the President many times, and I've written to Congress many times, to both our senators and congressmen in Washington and also our state representatives.
I've put stuff in letters to the editor, and I've talked to friends.
Today I think I signed about four or five online petitions to try to cut back on or to eliminate assault weapons that people are getting hold of.
So I've been involved in this problem, trying to talk people into doing something about it.
And as we know, our Congress is very obdurate about this.
They don't want to do anything, and I guess there are a lot of people in our country who want their guns.
So I'm discouraged, frankly.
And I have to admit also that I'm not able... the more of these events that happen, the less able I become to integrate them into my feeling life.
But I'm determined at least to witness what's happening and to not look away.
That's a Buddhist teaching as well, to realize that things are real when they are.
So I would like to open the floor to any of you who would like to speak to how you're feeling in these conditions.
If you have some ideas about what we might do, please offer them.
Anyone from any direction could begin speaking.
**Participant:** I used to think that the solution to our violence, to terrorism, was education.
Just open-mindedness, just being aware of others and who they are and their needs.

But when I was teaching my students several years ago, working with books about the Central Asian conflicts, I looked closely at that and realized that the 9-11, quote-unquote, pilots were highly educated, extremely well educated.
And this is true of many of the perpetrators of violence.
I find that my faith in education has been pulled up from underneath, and I haven't gotten beyond that yet.
But I, like you, am feeling a bit of despair about how much violence we hear of.
I mean, we're close to experiencing it even here in Bellingham.
Several would-be terrorists were apprehended up at Blaine.
There were several incidents of gun violence in Bellingham just recently.
And if it isn't education, if it isn't enough for caring people such as yourself, writing in their arguments, then what?
I live in one of the better parts of this [unclear: "very new state"].
I have a modest number of friends who are steadfast [unclear: "con owners"] and quite literally will give up their guns only when they're fired from their cold dead fingers.
And I have, especially on social media, been stuck in this maelstrom of ridiculous [unclear: "32nd memes"] from both sides that oversimplify this problem dramatically.
I've found it tremendously unhelpful, actually.
I mean, everybody's shouting and nobody's talking.
So I think that we have to start this conversation from a position where we realize that either side is going to give what they want.
And we have to start from a position of agreement that mass shootings are bad and that nobody wants mass shootings here.
Gun owner friends don't like mass shootings.
They don't want them to be around.
If we can start from that point, that we agree that we don't want people to experience this anymore, we can begin to work from there, from a point of agreement, to how we're going to accomplish that.
What we're doing right now is screaming at each other: give up assault rifles, versus you'll never get my assault rifle, I have a constitutional right to have one.
We're never going to get anywhere.
I think that we need to reframe the argument to how do we stop this.
I believe strongly in gun control myself, but I know I'm never going to get everything I want.
And I've signed all those petitions that you've signed.
But that is not going to go anywhere.
There's too much opposition.
So we have to come from a point where we realize we don't want this to happen.
We have to sit down and talk from the start there and see how we can get to something constructive.
I'm a gun owner, and I find it ridiculous that people can own a weapon like that.
I don't understand why somebody needs a weapon.
Assault?
Assault weapon.
I honestly understand what you're saying.
It's kind of weird.
I feel so assaulted even when they go to meet other gun owners.
I like to go to the range and shoot what we call the clinker, just a little thing to unwind, but I feel assaulted by now.
All my friends have assault rifles and they all want to have them, and I'm just like, do you really need that?
What is that for?
I don't get it.
It baffles me to this day.
It's baffled me since I first bought one.
I really don't understand, because you don't need it.
If you want to shoot targets, you don't need much.
And I get yelled at every day now.
It's a war right now between me and some of my friends, and it's really, really hard.
I don't know what to, I'm just very...
It's hard to know what to say about this, but it seems as though somehow we have to touch gun culture in this country.
Connect, own guns, and mindset and feelings are, I'm not a gun owner, but my grandfather was a gun owner and a hunter, and I really respected him.
I'm sure that this kind of thing that happened this weekend would be really important to him, from the standpoint of being a responsible gun owner.
There are certain things that came from his generation about being a responsible gun owner.
He had to have a lot of respect for what he was doing.
I remember my mother telling me a story about how she got just about in the worst trouble ever when somebody in deer camp had left a gun loaded, which was against the rules.

You weren't supposed to unload your gun before you came into camp, and she was fooling with the guy's gun for some reason, and it went off and blew a hole through my grandpa's door, his truck, and went into her book bag and lodged in her math book.
And she had to pay for that and explain it to her school teacher, as well as deal with my grandfather and whatnot.
It was somebody else's fault in a sense, but it was her fault too, and that was the level of responsible conduct that was looked upon around guns.
The message was, you really stepped over a line there.
But I remember after Sandy Hook, I was doing a trim job out in Ferndale, and there were some guys on the job too who were from the county, and I usually work in the county.
They were all talking about it, and they were all gun owners, and a couple of them owned AR-15s and that kind of thing.
They were basically all in the mode of trying to figure out how to buy as much ammo as they possibly could, a lifetime supply's worth.

They were literally figuring out how much do I shoot this gun, how much do I shoot that gun, so how many rounds do I need from now until the end of my life, because Obama's going to make it so that I'll never be [unclear: "up in the line"] anymore.

There was just a run on this, and they were sharing how they found places online where they could buy huge amounts, and other places where they were saying, oh, you can't get that anymore, it's all been bought out.
I was trying to ask them, why do you like that?
They said it was fun to shoot, and everything.
But it just seemed like those people were acting around guns and existing with guns in a fundamentally different way than my great-grandfather's era, that something has happened around gun culture.
We need to connect with gun culture and hopefully transform it from the inside, create a new ground: what is responsibility?
Because it seems to me that gun owners should be absolutely horrified that somebody who was investigated by the FBI was allowed to buy an AR-15.
As gun owners, they should feel like that's irresponsible gun ownership, rather than, well, a shift.
Hopefully this discussion that's happening now in the country is starting to peel back a layer of that a little bit.
But I think it's going to take people pushing the discussion beyond the forgetful point that happens after about two or three weeks, when they start forgetting about this.
Anyone who's sitting outside my view, please just go ahead and speak up.
I haven't given up on education.
It's a question of what kind of education, right?
There are so many different ways of using the mind and so many different ways of educating and being together.
It does seem like our dominant educational system has maybe for a long time, and I don't know if this has changed or what, had such an emphasis on separateness.
You get these skills to be employed in this way and to win the race.
So maybe education can be more transformational and more about connection and more about heart and more about understanding our feelings.
The thing that always strikes me about these events is the hard-to-parse reality that people only do stuff that makes sense to them.
We just do what makes sense to us, and somehow this action is what made sense to this fellow.
So I wonder about education and of course mental health services.
Who knows?
How big of a shift does it need to be?
Probably a pretty big shift.
It's about how we learn how to be a person, not just how to be an engineer or a school teacher or a good [unclear: "diamond talk writer"] or something like that.
How do we learn how to be a person?

And if we're really a person, maybe that kind of thing would never make sense to somebody. [unclear: "I still pray so."] So I think let's not give up on education, but let's ask ourselves, as educators and as friends of educators, how are your choices in the classroom, and how are our choices when we interact at the store or whatever, furthering the conversation of the heart?
Not just the conversation of skills and abilities and identities.
I'm glad you brought up education.
I would like to recommend compassion.
With each person, I think that goes a long way, and that is contagious.
I recognize that compassion alone won't end violence.
And I don't think weapons bans will end violence, and nothing you can name will end violence.
But really coming back to dealing with each person one at a time, trying to meet that person where they are and feeling that compassion, which gets really difficult sometimes.
There are times when I have five people standing in line to talk to me, and with the fifth person, there's this feeling of, man, can I really bring up compassion at the right time?
But then I think that when Avalokiteshvara meets the cries of the world, she doesn't meet them alone.
She's a conduit.
Okay.
Well, I haven't taken a lot of political action or outward action.
I have signed petitions.
But I think my work with this is close to home.
I look into myself and I see, well, what are the germs of violence in myself?
I watch my own anger at our political system that could allow this kind of thing to happen, and I watch that anger arise, and what are the consequences of my own anger?
How different am I from any of these other people?

And I watch my sense of righteousness in thinking that my position is better than their position, or thinking that the polarity is someplace out there and it's not within myself, and I haven't separated myself from this as well.
So I'm taking that work closer into myself and just trying to watch what's going on there, because I've got a lot of strong reactions, and the other reaction is kind of this doomsday reaction.

It's huge. [unclear: "It's Wednesday and we don't want to continue in the future."] But yet, when you think about washing your bowl, it also means every step, everything that you do in your daily life, you're attending to.

So that continues to be the practice, rather than allowing myself to get so obsessed or get this doomsday thinking in my head: to stay with whoever I am at the time and to be where I am at the time and do what I'm doing at the time.
That's what I've been trying to do.
I've found that true also, that being pulled out into what can we do in this complicated situation to make a difference, and then realizing I can be here now.
I can be with whom I'm with.
Someone has to do that, so it might as well be us who are being here now.
Others?
I'm finding a lot of resonance with everything people are saying, actually.
What's been stirring around in me, and has been for some time now, is how much the culture is changing and how much I share with all these people a deep sense of fear and vulnerability.
I wonder why people need to have assault rifles and all of the ammunition that they have, when it doesn't seem like it's just for self-protection or hunting.
I understand that they too share my fears about what will happen in the future and how they will take care of themselves.
I respond to that in a different kind of way, but I'm made of the same stuff.
That helps me feel, and makes me hopeful, as Kevin said, that somewhere deep inside there's a place to connect with, even if the conversation may be difficult.
I know that I have an opening and a common ground because I too see that suffering.
I'm thinking, too, that the willingness to come forward in that way is really important.
It's a little different, but it's been rattling around in my head, now that this happened in a gay nightclub, a gay and transgender nightclub.
I was around 40 years ago when Harvey Milk was assassinated at City Hall in San Francisco.
Events like that were pretty stunning at that point in time.
We're kind of [unclear: "a year to a single or two deaths"].
And I remember that Harvey Milk died putting his hand out, reaching for Dan White.
His teaching was to come out, to be visible, to be available, to not be afraid.

Somehow that gives me inspiration in pieces like this to be willing to try and make a connection and see what's really going on with the other person, and allow them to see I'm made of the same stuff that they are, even though I appear to be very different.
Which reminds me, your gay friends are feeling, I had forgotten to do this this time, but I'm very vulnerable right now.
Just any reassurance.
I know we won't let that happen to you, even though that's a lie and we can't prevent it, but we won't let that happen to you.
You're not alone.
You're not alone, whatever it is.
I kind of go off what Andrew was saying.
I just came here from a very [unclear: "gray area in a big state"].
I've been around guns all my life, and for a while it was part of a job description.
I think [unclear: "I've died of two shotguns"], one of which is my grandfather's shotgun and got through the Depression.
But I've had some luck.
I think Andrew is on to something.
We can sit here amongst us and we're kind of a homogeneous group, and we have a lot of the same thoughts and feelings about this.
But I've been talking to some of my friends back in southern Illinois who own AR-15s and a lot of other stuff, and fire guns and ammunition.
I've had some pretty good luck after one of these events bringing up that it wasn't that terrible, and them not saying anything about guns, and just saying, what do you think we should do about it?
And let them think about it and let them chew on it and listen to what they say.
I think that's it: instead of screaming, you guys don't need to have this, ask them what do you think we should do about it and get them to think.
I've seen more change or partial change in attitudes when I've asked that question than anything else.
But it's tough, like Andrew was saying.
You have to find somebody that doesn't agree with you and solicit their opinion and listen to them.
And that's not easy.
Well, we're here together supporting each other and all beings with compassion, we hope.
So thank you so much for being here.
Thank you.
And Andrea, did you have a final?
Okay.
I want you to close the talk.
Okay.
Okay.
